title: Can Border Quarantine Stop the Delta Variant? The Role of Vaccine Efficacy and Transmissibility
text:
Before the Delta variant, countries like Australia and New Zealand relied on strict border quarantine to keep COVID-19 out. This approach worked for earlier strains: rare breaches could be contained before they escalated into community outbreaks and costly lockdowns.
The arrival of the Delta variant changed this calculation. Delta spread much faster, caused more severe illness, and reduced how well vaccines worked. This raised a core policy question that this blog post explores: How do two key factors — viral transmissibility (how easily the virus spreads, measured by the basic reproduction number R₀) and vaccine efficacy (how well vaccines block infection and onward spread) — shape the ability of border quarantine systems to prevent outbreaks?

The arrival of the Delta variant changed this calculation. Delta spread much faster, caused more severe illness, and reduced how well vaccines worked. This raised a core policy question that this blog post explores: How do two key factors — viral transmissibility (how easily the virus spreads, measured by the basic reproduction number R₀) and vaccine efficacy (how well vaccines block infection and onward spread) — shape the ability of border quarantine systems to prevent outbreaks?

title: Can Border Quarantine Stop the Delta Variant? The Role of Vaccine Efficacy and Transmissibility
text:
Analysis
The evidence in this post comes from a 2022 modelling study by Zachreson and colleagues (Zachreson et al. 2022), who built an individual-based simulation of the Australian border quarantine system and paired it with a community transmission model. The team tested scenarios across a range of reproduction numbers (R₀, from 1 to 10) and vaccine efficacy levels (VE, from 0% to 90%).
The model also shows that community vaccination coverage is a critical multiplier of quarantine success: even when quarantine itself works, low population immunity means any breach will escalate rapidly.

Quarantine breach risk
Figure Figure 2 shows how the risk of a quarantine breach changes with viral transmissibility and vaccine efficacy. The colour scale represents total infection force relative to a pre-Delta, unvaccinated baseline — darker green means lower risk, brighter yellow means higher risk. The thick green line marks the baseline level: points below the line are safer than the unvaccinated pre-Delta scenario.
To read the chart: find the column for your chosen R₀ value on the x-axis, then move up to see how vaccine efficacy on the y-axis changes risk. The point where the green baseline line crosses is the minimum vaccine efficacy needed to keep breach risk at baseline levels.






Figure 1: Simplified heatmap of quarantine breach risk



Figure: Quarantine breach risk across viral transmissibility (R₀) and vaccine efficacy. Colour shows infection risk relative to a pre-Delta unvaccinated baseline; the thick green line marks the baseline level (1×). Values below the line are safer than baseline. Reproduced from Zachreson et al. (2022).






Figure 2: Quarantine breach risk across R₀ and vaccine efficacy



Adapted from Zachreson et al. (2022). The x-axis shows how contagious the virus is (R₀); the y-axis shows vaccine efficacy.
Two key patterns stand out:

Higher transmissibility demands higher vaccine efficacy. For a Delta-like R₀ of 6, vaccine efficacy must exceed roughly 50–55% just to keep breach risk at baseline levels. For an R₀ of 8, that threshold rises to around 65%.
Requirements saturate at very high R₀. Even for an R₀ of 10, the required vaccine efficacy levels off around 70–75%. This is because travellers in quarantine are grouped into small family cohorts, which puts a natural limit on how far internal transmission can spread — as long as basic infection control remains in place.



What drives these results?
Table 1 summarises how sensitive the model is to changes in key assumptions. This helps us understand which factors matter most for real-world quarantine performance.



Table 1: Sensitivity of quarantine performance to key parameter changes.










Factor
Scenario
Impact on quarantine efficacy

The most important takeaway from this sensitivity test is that infection control inside quarantine facilities is non-negotiable. If protocols break down and transmission within the facility spikes, even moderate vaccine efficacy cannot compensate for the increased breach risk.
Linking back to our opening question: the stronger the virus spreads, the more the system depends on both vaccines and well-run infection control. Quarantine alone cannot offset high transmissibility on its own.

title: Can Border Quarantine Stop the Delta Variant? The Role of Vaccine Efficacy and Transmissibility
text:
Conclusion
Returning to the question of whether border quarantine can stop Delta: it can, but only as part of a broader system. Three conclusions stand out:

Border quarantine cannot make up for low community vaccination. Even if every traveller and worker inside quarantine is fully vaccinated, a breach will still spread quickly in a community with low coverage. Quarantine buys time — it does not replace population immunity.
Vaccines that block transmission are far more valuable than vaccines that only prevent disease. As shown in Table Table 1, when vaccines primarily reduce onward transmission, the required efficacy threshold drops by roughly 20 percentage points.
Quarantine stringency should be calibrated to variant prevalence. The same measures that work for a low-transmissibility strain will be insufficient for a more infectious variant. Systems need built-in flexibility to tighten rules when more dangerous variants emerge.

These results are consistent with the wider evidence on border quarantine performance during the Delta wave of the COVID-19 pandemic (Zachreson et al. 2022). For policy analysts and students of public health, the broader lesson is clear: effective pandemic response relies on coordinated layers of protection, not any single measure in isolation.
